axes.question: Quelles aides, formations ou contacts extérieurs ont créé une capacité organisationnelle documentable sans établir un commandement externe ?
Les réseaux sociaux ont-ils modifié information, logistique et probabilité de participation, et avec quel niveau causal ?
Quelles preuves isolent l’effet marginal de l’aide extérieure ou des plateformes sur la chute du régime plutôt que sur la seule capacité ou participation ?

causal.counter: Programmes multiples et bénéficiaires hétérogènes; capacité ne vaut pas instruction opérationnelle.
causal.limit: Capacité institutionnelle fermée, tasking non inféré.
causal.mechanism: assistance démocratique extérieure -> ressources/capacité de société civile

causal.causal_right: formation identifiée -> retour en Égypte -> enseignement de tactiques non violentes
causal.limit: Transfert de méthode établi pour un acteur; effet marginal sur le soulèvement non isolé.
causal.mechanism: formation CANVAS -> apprentissage tactique -> transmission interne à April 6

causal.causal_right: usage social media -> information/logistique -> probabilité accrue de participation initiale
causal.limit: Association multivariée forte et mécanisme plausible; pas d’assignation randomisée ni effet sur issue du régime.
causal.mechanism: usage réseaux sociaux -> information/logistique -> participation au premier jour en Égypte

causal.gap: Les études sont rétrospectives/perceptives et le mouvement naît localement à Sidi Bouzid; absence de contrefactuel sans réseaux sociaux.
causal.limit: Catalyse informationnelle/coalition soutenue; déclenchement et résultat non isolés.
causal.mechanism: réseaux sociaux -> coalition/mobilisation -> chute de régime en Tunisie

causal.gap: Pas de chaîne unique de commandement ni de design identifiant l’effet marginal sur la survie du régime.
causal.limit: Contributions intermédiaires documentées; causalité générale du changement de régime non établie.
causal.mechanism: assistance extérieure + plateformes -> soulèvement -> changement de régime

claims.claim: Une infrastructure substantielle d’assistance démocratique américaine existait en Égypte avant 2011 et finançait des capacités de société civile, participation et médias.
Un transfert tactique transnational de méthodes de mobilisation non violente vers au moins un militant d’April 6 est documenté avant 2011.
L’assistance occidentale documentée établit que les États-Unis ont commandé ou orchestré le soulèvement égyptien de janvier 2011.
claims.gap: Aucune instruction authentifiée reliant un financeur/État à la décision de lancer, au plan opérationnel ou à l’issue du soulèvement; le câble cité doute lui-même d’un plan coordonné.

claims.claim: En Égypte, les réseaux sociaux ont facilité information, logistique et participation précoce aux manifestations.
En Tunisie, Facebook et les réseaux sociaux ont contribué à l’information, aux réseaux et à la formation d’une coalition protestataire, sans être démontrés comme déclencheur unique.
L’assistance extérieure ou les plateformes suffisent à expliquer causalement la chute des régimes lors des printemps arabes.
claims.gap: Les données ferment des mécanismes de capacité, diffusion et participation mais pas le contrefactuel de régime; répression, griefs locaux, coalitions et décisions des élites restent des causes concurrentes non isolées.

controls.control: audience numérique != mobilisation de rue réussie
participation accrue != chute du régime attribuable

facts.subject: U.S. democracy assistance in Egypt before 2011
facts.value: GAO reports about $154.8 million in governance/justice/democracy funding allocated to Egypt over FY2006-2008, placing Egypt among the larger recipients outside Iraq/Afghanistan.

facts.subject: Content of U.S. democracy assistance
facts.value: U.S. democracy assistance programs included civic participation, civil-society strengthening, media freedom/freedom of information and related governance activities; funding was implemented through USAID, State DRL and NED structures.

facts.subject: Egypt social media and first-day protest participation
facts.value: A survey of Tahrir participants found that, controlling for other factors, social-media use greatly increased the odds a respondent attended protests on the first day; information was primarily interpersonal via Facebook, phone or face-to-face contact.

facts.subject: Egypt protest media production
facts.value: About half of surveyed Tahrir participants produced and disseminated visual material from demonstrations, mainly through Facebook, documenting an information/amplification function distinct from regime-change causality.

facts.subject: 2008 Facebook mobilization negative control
facts.value: The April 6 Facebook page rapidly accumulated roughly 70,000 followers in 2008, yet planned solidarity protests largely fizzled outside Mahalla under repression and organizational uncertainty, showing online reach was not sufficient for successful street mobilization.

facts.subject: CANVAS tactical training transfer
facts.value: April 6 activist Mohamed Adel traveled to Serbia in 2009 and received training in nonviolent organization and street-mobilization tactics associated with CANVAS/Otpor, then returned to Egypt and trained others.

facts.subject: Reported U.S.-financed democracy training links
facts.value: A contemporaneous report republished by IRI stated that Arab activists, including figures linked to Egypt’s April 6 movement, had received training or support from U.S.-financed democracy organizations; this establishes a reported support network, not an authenticated command chain.

facts.subject: April 6 activist contact with U.S. officials
facts.value: A 2008 U.S. diplomatic cable records an April 6 activist’s participation in an Alliance of Youth Movements summit and meetings with U.S. officials and think tanks; the embassy explicitly expressed doubt about his claim of a coordinated opposition transition plan.

facts.subject: Tunisia Facebook perceived catalyst
facts.value: A post-revolution online survey of 333 Tunisian Internet users identified political, informational and media-platform functions through which respondents perceived Facebook as a catalyst in the revolution.

facts.subject: Tunisia social media coalition mechanisms
facts.value: Research using expert interviews and a web survey of 608 Tunisian Facebook users argues that social media helped build networks, circumvent the media blackout, mitigate collective-action problems and support a national protest identity.

facts.subject: Tunisia e-revolution caution
facts.value: Lecomte describes Internet/social-media use as a catalyst for a protest movement born in Sidi Bouzid while warning against the e-revolution narrative that treats social networks as the triggering cause.

facts.subject: Post-2011 U.S. democracy assistance and NGO trial
facts.value: GAO found that Egypt’s prosecution of four U.S. NGOs significantly disrupted U.S. democracy-and-governance assistance after 2011; the U.S. government provided diplomatic, legal and grant-flexibility support, demonstrating an assistance infrastructure without proving orchestration of the 2011 uprising.

facts.subject: Temporal control on NED Arab Spring response
facts.value: NED describes responding to the Arab Spring as a priority in 2011 and continued a broad global grants program; post-uprising expansion or response cannot by itself be back-projected as evidence of pre-uprising tasking.

attempt_history.mnemo_row: MNEMO_UNAVAILABLE — local memory service not available; no memory ids fabricated.

persistence.mnemo_row: MNEMO_UNAVAILABLE — local memory service not available; no memory ids fabricated.

run.scope: Cas sélectionnés 2010–2013 où les flux et actions sont documentables. Tracer acteur extérieur -> ressource/formation/plateforme/diplomatie -> bénéficiaire ou audience -> action de mobilisation -> exposition/participation -> effet politique. Prioriser archives, programmes d’aide, données de plateformes, communications diplomatiques, chronologies et études causales. Gardes : soutien != déclenchement ; réseau social != révolution ; financement != contrôle ; simultanéité != coordination ; changement de régime != effet attribuable à un seul mécanisme.

CONTRADICTION_LEDGER.issue: reports of U.S.-financed training versus lack of authenticated tasking
CONTRADICTION_LEDGER.resolution: retain support-network fact; do not infer command or funding of the uprising

CONTRADICTION_LEDGER.issue: large Facebook audience in 2008 but weak street result
CONTRADICTION_LEDGER.resolution: use as direct sufficiency control against online reach = mobilization

CONTRADICTION_LEDGER.issue: Tunisia studies call Facebook catalyst while warning against e-revolution myth
CONTRADICTION_LEDGER.resolution: separate information/coalition mechanism from trigger/outcome causality

CONTRADICTION_LEDGER.issue: post-2011 U.S./NED response may be mistaken for pre-event design
CONTRADICTION_LEDGER.resolution: enforce temporal ordering; post-event response cannot establish prior orchestration

CREDO.rule: prove each edge separately: assistance -> capacity -> adoption -> mobilization -> political outcome

DIALECTICAL_MAP.antithesis: Les soulèvements partent de griefs et coalitions domestiques; outils et formations ne déterminent ni déclenchement ni issue.
DIALECTICAL_MAP.synthesis: Capacités externes, transfert tactique et facilitation numérique sont établis dans des cas bornés; aucune chaîne ne ferme une orchestration externe ou une causalité générale sur la chute des régimes.
DIALECTICAL_MAP.thesis: Assistance occidentale et réseaux transnationaux/numériques ont contribué matériellement aux soulèvements.

established: CANVAS tactical transfer to at least one April 6 activist
social-media facilitation of first-day participation/logistics in Egypt
not_established: external assistance as sufficient cause of regime change
partial: extent of U.S.-financed training links to April 6 as an organization
marginal contribution of tactical training to mobilization

assumptions: les montants d’aide prouvent une infrastructure mais pas un bénéficiaire particulier
les enquêtes de manifestants identifient participation/logistique mieux que l’issue du régime
les récits organisationnels et journalistiques sur formation exigent un plafond causal

implicit.I01: transfert de capacité peut être réel sans principal commanditaire
implicit.I02: outils numériques réduisent des coûts sans déterminer l’issue
implicit.I03: chronologie distingue soutien préexistant et réponse post-soulèvement

MANIPULATION_REPORT.query_guidance: archives publiques, documents de financement, câbles, études académiques; utiliser les récits militants comme preuve bornée de formation/adoption, pas de causalité générale

rhetorical.R02: réduire une coalition à un outil numérique
rhetorical.R03: attribuer l’issue à un mécanisme intermédiaire

speaker.goal: tester les chaînes externes et numériques des printemps arabes
speaker.target: séparer capacité, mobilisation et changement de régime

negative_results: no authenticated U.S. command chain to launch uprising
online reach not sufficient for street success
MODULE_EXECUTION.reason: separate exposure, logistics, participation and outcome

negative_results: post-2011 support cannot prove pre-2011 orchestration
not_computable: latent informal pre-event contacts beyond records
operations_applied: ordered pre-2011 aid, 2011 uprising, post-2011 program response

NEXT_QUERIES: To close external orchestration, require authenticated instructions tying a funder/state to launch timing, operational plan and beneficiary compliance.
To estimate platform causal effect, seek exogenous outages or stronger quasi-experimental variation linked to protest participation and outcome.
For synthesis, retain capacity/training/platform mechanisms separately from trigger and regime-change claims.

flows: US democracy assistance -> civil-society/media capacities in Egypt
limits: platform use does not identify regime outcome

RESPONSIBILITY_MAP.documented_action: financed democracy/civil-society/media programs in Egypt before 2011
RESPONSIBILITY_MAP.scope: capacity support; uprising tasking not established

RESPONSIBILITY_MAP.documented_action: trained at least one April 6 activist in nonviolent organizing tactics
RESPONSIBILITY_MAP.scope: training transfer; regime-change causality not established

RESPONSIBILITY_MAP.documented_action: facilitated information/logistics and were associated with early protest participation
RESPONSIBILITY_MAP.scope: mechanism of communication/coordination, not intentional principal

RESPONSIBILITY_MAP.documented_action: converted grievances/networks into street mobilization under repression
RESPONSIBILITY_MAP.scope: domestic causal structure incompletely measured here

SCOPING_REPORT.reason: bounded cases with traceable resource/platform mechanisms and explicit controls

breaks: 2008 April 6 mobilisation Facebook et échec partiel hors Mahalla
TEMPORAL_STATE.window: Égypte/Tunisie principalement 2006-2013, avec études rétrospectives ultérieures

VERIFICATION_REPORT.method: official funding records + diplomatic archive + academic participation studies + bounded training accounts + explicit negative controls
negative_checks: 2008 April 6 Facebook mobilization fizzled outside Mahalla
VERIFICATION_REPORT.verdict: sufficient for capacity/training/platform facilitation; insufficient for external orchestration or general regime-change causality
